query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a small fraction of a ductility-enhancing element (e.g., chromium) into the equiatomic NbMoTaW alloy will improve its room-temperature ductility and irradiation resistance while preserving its high‐temperature mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW with excellent high-temperature strength but poor room-temperature ductility and unvalidated (experimentally) irradiation resistance.
generation.intervention: Partial substitution of one element (e.g., replacing ~5–15% of the overall atomic content) with chromium to form a NbMoTaWCr alloy in a non-equiatomic ratio.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests conducted at room temperature (for ductility evaluation) and at 1600 °C (to confirm high-temperature performance) along with controlled helium-ion irradiation experiments at energies relevant to previously studied refractory HEAs.
generation.structural_mediator: A modified BCC lattice with increased lattice distortion that promotes the activation of additional slip systems and enhances defect recombination during irradiation.
generation.mechanism: Chromium addition is expected to lower the Peierls barrier for dislocation motion, thereby improving ductility at low temperatures while its presence increases compositional complexity. This, in turn, may enhance atomic diffusion and defect recombination, mitigating irradiation-induced damage (such as blistering or amorphization) without compromising the BCC phase stability at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated equiatomic NbMoTaW alloy, the NbMoTaWCr variant should exhibit improved room-temperature ductility and reduced irradiation-induced defects (e.g., lower blistering and defect accumulation) while retaining comparable high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: This intervention is intended to be effective in the room-temperature regime (improving ductility) and remain stable up to 1600 °C; under helium-ion irradiation conditions analogous to those previously studied in refractory HEAs.
generation.uncertainty: The precise chromium content required for the optimal balance of ductility and irradiation resistance is not well defined, and potential effects on phase stability at extreme conditions require experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of NbMoTaWCr alloys with varying Cr fractions (e.g., 5%, 10%, and 15% substitution). Conduct room-temperature tensile tests, high-temperature (1600 °C) mechanical tests, and controlled helium-ion irradiation experiments. Characterize the microstructure before and after irradiation using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and assess surface blistering.
measurements: Tensile stress-strain curves at room temperature
TEM-based defect density and microstructural analysis post-irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the NbMoTaWCr alloys do not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility and/or do not exhibit reduced irradiation-induced defects (compared to the baseline NbMoTaW), or if high-temperature performance degrades significantly, then the hypothesis is falsified.

chosen.approach: Alloy composition tuning for improved ductility and irradiation resistance
